children.text:
The Story of the Moth

One night, the whole family had gone to bed early-except for my
mother and me. I don't know why, but the two of us stayed up,
sitting quietly together.

The candles were already put out using a curved tin blower. The
room was dim, lit only by a coconut oil lamp.

That night, my mother was teaching me how to read a book called El
Amigo de los Niños. She grew impatient because I was reading
poorly. She also scolded me for drawing silly pictures in the book.

Then she said, "Just listen," and began to read aloud herself.

I got tired of listening to words I didn't understand. I turned my eyes
to the little flame instead. It danced cheerfully. Some small moths
were flying around it in circles.

I happened to yawn. My mother saw that I was losing interest, so she
stopped reading.

"I'll read you a very nice story now," she said.

"You must listen."

I opened my eyes wide. This sounded new and exciting. She began
reading a fable about an old moth and a young moth, translating it
into Tagalog as she read.

From the very first sentence, I was interested. I stared at the lamp
and watchede the moths flying around it.

The story was like this:

A mother moth once warned her daughter not to go near a flame. The
light may look beautiful and inviting, but it was dangerous. It could
burn anyone who got too close.

The mother moth said she herself had once flown too near the flame
and barely escaped. She had half-burned her wings.

The young moth promised to obey. But soon, she began to wonder,

"Why is my mother trying to scare me? Why should I close my eyes to
such a pretty light?"

"Old people are always afraid of everything! What harm can it do me
if I go near-just carefully? I'll have such a good story to tell if I look
closer."

So she flew around the flame. At first, it felt pleasantly warm. That
gave her more courage, so she flew closer and closer.

But then she got too near. Dazzled by the light, she fell into the flame
and died.

As my mother tucked me into bed, she said:

"Don't be like the young moth. Don't disobey, or you may get hurt the
same way."

I don't remember if I answered her. But the story opened my eyes.

I never saw moths the same way again. They were no longer just
small insects. Now I believed they could talk. They could warn and
give advice-just like my mother.

The flame also looked different to me. It seemed more beautiful. It
glowed brighter and felt more magical. I finally understood why
moths flew around the light.

-THE END-
